_readme: TUNING, research only (rule 38g). The twenty style-guide fields of rule 114a (records/BOHEMIA_RESEARCH_HOW_NOT_TO_LOOK_VIBE_CODED_ROUND_ONE_10_16_26.md, Section C)
as four 2D studios set them: Battle Brothers (Overhype), Dead Cells (Motion Twin), Blasphemous (The Game Kitchen), Eastward (Pixpil).
Every cell is one of three things: a number or rule WITH its source URL; 'not published' when no developer source states it; or an INFERENCE marked as one.
The web was egress-blocked from this machine (CONNECT 403, 10/18, the same wall DIRECTION hit 9/28), so every cell comes from search snippets of the named page, never a fetched page.
A cell with confidence 'secondary' or 'community' is not a studio statement. DIRECTION picks; nothing here is a ruling. Nothing in the game reads this file.
Rendered by tools/bohemia_tuning_twenty_fields_page.py into the record and the VOTE page.
ours_source: rule 114a (Section C examples, illustrative), rule 115 (the rig), laws/BOHEMIA_LAW_THE_GROUND_MAY_ZOOM_THE_PERSON_MAY_NOT_9_21_26.md, records/BOHEMIA_THE_MASTER_RIG_ROUND_THREE_THE_LOOK_AT_THE_SOURCE_10_17_26.md, records/BOHEMIA_BB_DENSITY_THE_MAP_FLOOR_9_28_26.md

bb.v: Painted busts, 'somewhat more serious and gritty, but still exaggerated' (moved there from 'light-hearted comic'); the detailed painted look kept by layering gear instead of animating.

dc.v: Three pillars: 'a saturated color palette, Celtic architecture and the theme of alchemy'; 'a modern take on this art style' with particles, motion, a 3D lighting system and shaders.

bl.v: 'Purist' pixel art: 'there is nothing in Blasphemous that is not pixel art'; no shaders, no 3D elements; Spanish religious art (Ribera, Velazquez, Zurbaran, Murillo) and Seville.

ew.v: 'Retro Pixel Art + 3D Lighting' (the studio's own line, 2015); 'a 3D game with a 2D perspective'.

fields.ours: Rule 114a's example line plus rule 115: modelled at the source, rendered to pixels through the rig; analog horror on every pixel.

bb.v: No pixel grid: painted raster at the screen's native resolution, one painted pixel per screen pixel, with separate UI-scale and scene-scale sliders. Icons painted at 500x500 and resized to 48x48. A sprite's size is set by its brush metadata offsets (the 104x142 width/height in the docs' example 'do nothing').

dc.v: 640x360 (a developer-adjacent list, not a studio page). The hero is 'only about 50 pixels tall'; the mesh is rendered 'in a very small size and without antialiasing'.

bl.v: 640x360 native, pixel-perfect at integer multiples; in development 'a virtual frame resolution of a fixed 360 pixel height' with the width from the monitor's aspect ratio, pixel-perfect or stretched upscaling as a player option.

ew.v: Not published by Pixpil. Players measure a 360p base, the PC build locked at 720p at launch with linear filtering on non-integer scales (a community thread, not a studio statement).

fields.ours: The person is one size everywhere, a 112 box about 100 px painted; the rig draws 128 px a metre, a 1.72 m man 66x132 px; a 96 px tile floor. No internal canvas is declared; the demo draws at device pixels.

bb.v: Hex grid, busts only: 'the top half of each character, without animation', one facing, gear swapped in layers because 'drawing each character in several directions would have multiplied the workload immensely'; the world map painted from above.

dc.v: Side view platformer; backgrounds drawn as pixel art and 'redrawn in normal maps' so 3D lights work on a flat scene.

bl.v: Side view, no 3D elements anywhere.

ew.v: Top-down three-quarter; 'smart placing and orientation of the sprite to make it look like 3D'; each asset split by 'its natural structure' and rebuilt in a 3D environment before lighting.

fields.ours: 45 degree three-quarter (the 45 DEGREE ART LAW), a square grid (the third votes).

bb.v: Not published. The only palette note is a development one: 'the strong colors are just for differentiating the regions better during development' (placeholders, not the look).

dc.v: No palette file published. The rule is a direction: saturation pushed 'almost exclusively' in the midtones; complementary schemes indoors 'to give a confined feeling', analogous outdoors for depth; the dynamic light tints a level 'while keeping its base colors'.

bl.v: Not published (the 200-page art book is the likely home; not reachable from here).

ew.v: Not published. The final colours are graded after lighting: the engine adds 'LUT texture' colour grading, SSAO and an optional CRT blur on top of the sprites.

fields.ours: No master palette file yet (rule 114a owes it). The rig snaps a render's colours 0.6 of the way toward the pack family's colours; people and beasts have no family yet.

bb.v: None. Painted raster, thousands of colours per sprite. The one size rule is for icons: at 48x48 'it all comes down to colors and contrasts when you resize it'.

dc.v: None fixed per sprite. Each frame ships with a normal map and is lit by a toon shader and dynamic lights, so on-screen colours are the light's, not a count the artist set.

bl.v: Not published. INFERENCE: hand-placed pixels with no shaders imply a hand-chosen palette per sprite, the only one of the four where a per-sprite count could even be measured on screen.

ew.v: None published. Deferred lights plus a LUT change every screen colour, so a count on a screenshot is a count of the lighting.

fields.ours: Rule 114a's example caps (12 / 6 / 5 / 24) are illustrative. The rig's round three renders measured 10,146 to 13,047 colours per sheet, and DIRECTION wrote 'his art is not limited-palette'. THE FINDING: see section 3.

bb.v: Not published for the busts (static paintings). The map has a day/night cycle that changes the light and the play (night slows parties and cuts sight range); its direction is not stated.

dc.v: No fixed direction: dynamic 3D lights over per-frame normal maps, 'a torch can light a statue from the correct side'. The normal maps for backgrounds are drawn by hand.

bl.v: Baked into the pixels; no runtime light. Direction not published.

ew.v: No fixed direction: 'general deferred shading, which enables our designer to put more lights into the level'; a hand-painted bump map per asset part; weather and time of day move the light.

fields.ours: One hard light in the rig (rule 115d); the gate measures light top-to-bottom per render (round three: light +8.7 on the truck).

bb.v: Painted gradients, no step count; after the resize an icon gets 'smart sharpen 35%' and '+20 brightness +20 contrast'.

dc.v: Stepped by a 'basic toon shader' over the normal map; 'cell shading techniques when rendering models in low resolution and without applying anti-aliasing'.

bl.v: Hand pixel shading, frame by frame; steps not published.

ew.v: Lit by the bump map and the lights, plus a simulated SSAO pass; steps not published.

fields.ours: Clay shading in the rig: roughness at least 0.9, specular 0.15, metallic at most 0.2, grime from the model's own ambient occlusion (round three).

bb.v: Not published. INFERENCE: painted busts carry no pixel outline.

dc.v: Not published; no search result describes an outline pass.

bl.v: Not published.

ew.v: Not published.

fields.ours: Rule 114a's example (1 px selout on people, none on tiles). The rig's own measure is an EDGE score (-35 to +7 passes; a ring 20% darker reads -45, a fault).

bb.v: Fully anti-aliased by nature (painted raster scaled by the engine).

dc.v: No AA: rendered 'without antialiasing'. The named leftover is 'flickering pixels', which 'could be eliminated manually, but the whole point of the process is speed'; 'we still haven't found any solution'.

bl.v: Hand-placed pixels; no shader AA. Dither rule not published.

ew.v: Pixel art in Aseprite; an optional CRT blur filter on top; dither rule not published.

fields.ours: The rig's round-three fault list: 'airbrushed at 4x' is a fail; grain finer than a pixel averages to grey; even grain is a leopard print.

bb.v: Large heads and prominent facial features, 'an exaggerated, almost caricature style'; 'the smaller a figure gets, the more iconic and readable it has to be'; weapon icons 'not drawn to real proportions' so they read from far.

dc.v: Hero about 50 px tall; the models kept simple because of it; attacks are pose-to-pose and 'VFX' carry 'movement, strength, and power'.

bl.v: 'Large sprites and smooth animation' (a secondary description; the frame height is not published; one fan comment asks if it is 64x64, unanswered).

ew.v: Not published.

fields.ours: A 1.72 m man is 66x132 px, a quarter of a 96x96 tile's area; on a 390x844 phone at 1x the 100 px person is about 12% of the screen's height (Dead Cells' 50 px hero on a 360 frame is 14%).

bb.v: Paint small: 'scaling down large images can even result in a lower overall quality. All the downscaled details can make the final icon noisy and hard to read'. The busts' detail is paid for by not animating them.

dc.v: The model is cheap because 'the character's height in the game is only 50 pixels'; the detail is spent on VFX and particles instead.

bl.v: 'Limited by the pixel art style, by the size of the screen, by the graphics'; no budget number published.

ew.v: Not published.

fields.ours: Rule 114a's example (hero 40%, mid 25%, background 10% with a flat rest region of 25%); not yet a number of ours.

bb.v: World tiles 'completely reworked' together with 'the way they are combined to achieve a more natural look'; characters are stacked layers (head, helmet, weapon swapped independently); a bust ships with damaged and dead variants (bust_body_southern_01 and its damaged and dead files).

dc.v: The 3D pipe lets one animation be reused across different models; backgrounds tinted per biome by the light instead of redrawn.

bl.v: Not published.

ew.v: Not published.

fields.ours: Rule 114a's example (two variants per tile 70/20/10, no run over four, two wear decals per prop).

bb.v: The anchor is written: 'for units on the battlefield, the center point is the tile at the bottom'; a cast shadow rule is not published.

dc.v: Not published.

bl.v: Not published.

ew.v: Not published (the deferred lights cast the contact).

fields.ours: Rule 114a's example (a 1 px contact line one ramp step darker along the footprint); the rig's own shadow is the model's ambient occlusion.

bb.v: A UI-scale slider separate from the scene scale; skill icons 48x48 (sharpened and punched after the resize); item icons 70x70 in the stash and 70x140 in the character window; every new icon is checked against the existing ones.

dc.v: Not published.

bl.v: Not published (the art director's first job was 'a general UI designer').

ew.v: Not published.

fields.ours: Rule 114a: the project's pixel font, no gradients, blur or glow, radius 0 or 1, no system fonts, the same HUD at every zoom (UI [no browser defaults on the HUD]).

bb.v: None on the busts: 'without animation' by design.

dc.v: Keys first: 'once, and only once, the animation is convincing and correctly timed with the least amount of frames possible, I add interpolation frames'; attacks 'essentially pose-to-pose' with VFX. A third-party claim of 8 to 12 frames per attack is unverified.

bl.v: Hand drawn frame by frame in Photoshop, new frames 'by manipulating current ones'; pencil drafts by Juan Miguel first; played through Unity's PowerSprite Animator. No frame rate published.

ew.v: Not published.

fields.ours: 120 BPM, 12 keys a bar, a joint never reverses more than 120 degrees between drawn keys (the envelope law); the rig steps frames with no motion blur (rule 115d).

bb.v: No page published. The live version: the artist 'goes back and forth to check whether the icon is clearly readable and how it compares to the already existing icons'.

dc.v: Not published.

bl.v: Not published.

ew.v: Not published.

fields.ours: Rule 114a owes one pair per field 4 to 14; none exists.

bb.v: 'Noisy' (downscaled detail that makes an icon hard to read).

dc.v: 'Flickering pixels' (the one named defect of the 3D-to-pixel pipe, never fully solved).

bl.v: Not published.

ew.v: Not published.

fields.ours: Rule 114a's list of eleven; the rig's round three named three of its own (too few colours under one sun, a ring too dark, airbrushed grain).

bb.v: Readability wins: faces must stay readable at the most zoomed-out level, so figures get more iconic and weapons leave real proportion.

dc.v: Speed wins over cleanup: flickering pixels are left because 'the whole point of the process is speed'.

bl.v: Purity wins: nothing on screen that is not pixel art, even where it costs.

ew.v: The light wins over the pixel's own colour: the sprite is split and bump-mapped so the lights, weather and time of day decide the final colour.

fields.ours: Rule 114a's example: readability at 1x, then palette over detail, then silhouette over colour. Rule 115 adds the source: one rig, everything the same.

bb.v: Judge at the final size: paint rough at 500x500, resize to 48x48, compare against the existing icons, then sharpen and punch.

dc.v: Time the keys with the fewest frames until they convince, then interpolate; clean flickers by hand only where it is worth the time.

bl.v: Concept sketch, pencil animation draft, pixel frames, then tuning in the engine's sprite animator.

ew.v: Asset in Aseprite, split by structure, rebuilt in 3D, bump map painted per part, then into the engine under the lights.

fields.ours: Rule 114a's example (contact sheet at 1x, real background, greyscale, 8x8 silhouette row, in the game, the gate report attached); the rig has four sheets at 1:1 and a look sheet (round three).

bb.v: A key visual painted as the target, and the move away from the comic look: the anti-reference is their own first assets, 'made in short late-night sessions and later redone'.

dc.v: Celtic architecture and alchemy as the two visual pillars beside the palette.

bl.v: Spanish religious painting of past centuries, Seville's architecture and processions; 'dark and macabre but also carried a beautiful side'.

ew.v: Not published beyond the setting.

fields.ours: The analog horror bible, the Newgrounds era, the runway names, the creepy claymation kids' show (rule 115d); the anti-reference: the three-card grid, the purple panel, the default pack.
